Name: Porco Rosso
Review: day 10/movie 10 “i’d rather be a pig than a fascist”  beautiful little piece that manages to both reflect on the tragedy of a veterans postwar life AND make me go hahahaha hehehehe look at the little piggy fly around  “i’m a pig. i don’t fight for honor, i fight for a paycheck”   porco is a pig to everyone in his life  -to the pirates, he is war vet constantly looking to take them down and ruin their paydays -to italy and the fascist secret police, he is a defector who betrayed his country  -to his fellow sea plane pilots, he’s just a good bounty hunter with little regard for honor  -to gina, he is a changed man after the war, unwilling to accept his love, and constantly breaking women’s hearts  to me, gina and him have the most interesting and probably the most complex relationship in the movie. porco sees how gina idolizes his past, using his old name in conversation, and adores the last picture of his former self. porco, however, just wants to be accepted, and seeing how the most important woman in his life thinks more of his past than his current pigly self only lowers his self esteem and makes him feel incapable of that love. the truth however, is just that gina remembers porco caring for her more as a human, and although she accepts him as a pig and still loves him, he doesn’t know how to accept that as he could when he was human.  and fio, on the other hand, sees him not as a pig but as a role model. fio is the only one to see him human since the war, as fio enjoys porco for who he is, reinvigorating his sense of purpose by forcing him to fight for her. she sees porco as a human because not only does she not see him as a pig, but as a father figure to her, he does not see himself as a pig either  - all that combined with stunning animation, incredible dogfights, and of course a pig flying a plane, make this some of miyazaki’s best work ye tldr i love when the silly pig flies around he’s a lil goofball

Name: Raging Bull
Review:
shittiest underdog story ever (small spoilers ahead)

easily the most conflicted i have felt about whether i liked a movie or not in a while - dragged HARD at times (was tired though) and there were so many punches. lamotta is a really interesting guy and it’s fun to kind of get inside his mind(never “going down”, crying after the throw, the whole self hatred thing), but also it’s just like cmon dude you suck. 

thought i was going to hate the ending but ended up liking it a lot, the crash from a self-important, larger-than-life club owner with everything he wants to a lonely, emotionally stunted man in prison felt fitting. going from begging his brother to hit him to begging him to kiss him is a nice little way to tie the sad little bow on the whole story

i think that this movie is easy to dislike or feel meh about at first because of the inclination to look for a way to feel even a tiny bit sympathetic towards lamotta, and there is absolutely nothing there. it’s so easy to just chalk it up to “oh this guy blows” and then see if there’s anything else interesting going on, but there really isn’t sometimes. lamotta doesn’t need a character arc because it isn’t about his redemption or him winning, it’s about how horrible he is- there can’t be any kind of acceptance of that fact because he always knows it, he just never changes. the conflict/resolution isn’t found in his boxing, any growth he has as a person, but instead the people around him, who each learn to cut him out. as lamotta’s life changes, losing his brother and wife, his boxing career and status, it becomes painfully clear how stubbornly stagnant he is internally 

also obviously helps that de niro and scorsese are both always amazing and joe pesci is an acting hero

Name: La Haine
Review:
Might be a perfect movie-- been meaning to watch this for a while and finally got a good enough excuse to throw it on (had to watch it for french class). incredibly annoyed that I can't sit around and stew in this one for the rest of the night and that I won't be able to get into it on why this movie is awesome with my french prof pq i'm buns at french. 

not sure exactly what to take away from this one but the first thoughts that popped into my head(aside from 'oh holy shit') were that we see Vinz angry over Abdel at the start of the movie and its meant to seem excessive and a little crazy- he's a character we have no attachment to, so we brush off his anger. Then when Vinz is killed, he is someone we've learned about and now that same anger and shock is passed to the audience, who hope the gunshot at the end is Hubert killing the cop. 

Because we've put a face (and some sympathy) towards Vinz, the audience is aware of and possibly complicit in the hatred that is one of many roots of the cycle of banlieue violence. It would go totally against Hubert's character and beliefs to kill that cop. One of his strongest convictions in the movie was that hate breeds hate, and he was looking to leave the banlieue, believing it was making him crazy. He wanted to leave the vicious cycle, but in order for him to shoot the cop, he would be succumbing to it, someone with a plan to get out forced to go against his beliefs and reduced to another name in a violent headline. 

Despite that, the audience is forced to hope that that's the outcome, since as we see it, the only other option is death. We are meant to think 'Jusqu’ici tout va bien' as the movie progresses, simply taking in the environment and characters- it isn't taken by the film as much more than a passing thought, but Hubert is the only character who contemplates leaving, trying to avoid the craziness they are surrounded by. No one else acknowledges the situation they are stuck in, thinking only 'so far so good', and we are then made to hope Hubert has become a killer. IMO french movies are often built on engaging directly with the audience, something La Haine accomplishes by manipulating the viewer, pulling them into the hatred and violence it condemns.

Name: Obsession
Review:
girlfriend was enjoying the movie i was TWEAKED tf out the whole time

obviously really scary but this is one of the only movies i’ve watched and had a visceral reaction to, obviously possessed nikki is creepy but the presence of real nikki trying to push back and eventually giving up was the glue for 90% of the good horror (the initial jumpscare where she freaks tf out when in bed with him the first time is maybe the most i’ve ever jumped at a movie and just sets you up to be on the edge of your seat the entire movie, and the one of nikki sleeping toward the climax is probably the toughest to watch). 

horror centering on the loss of autonomy is nothing new, but the person doing it being a friend instead of like evilgod the demon from hell is a fun twist— bear is totally a victim here too but the way he misinterprets that victimhood is interesting. A much less compelling movie that i would want to see is if it wasn’t the fucked-up wish trope and nikki falls in normal love w bear but is still ‘trapped’ as possessed nikki. Bear clearly regrets making the wish almost immediately, but he neglects this bc he has what he wants until she cooks the cat etc etc. 

I think the thing that sat with me the most after leaving was wondering how that version would go, how nikki’s temporary freak-outs look, how bear reacts to it, if the people around them would still find it as weird as they do. idk if this is a hot take or not but i feel like that version, even if not as scary, retains about 90% of the stuff about this movie that freaked me the fuck out TLDR possession is freaky
